youtube.title: Ignaz Semmelweis: Why Doctors Refused to Wash Their Hands
youtube.description:
Ignaz Semmelweis found out why mothers were dying in Vienna's best maternity ward, and the answer was the doctors' own hands.

Vienna General Hospital, 1846: in the First Clinic, run by doctors and medical students, about one mother in nine died of childbed fever, while the midwives' Second Clinic lost fewer than three in a hundred. Women begged not to be admitted, and street births were safer than the ward. Then Jakob Kolletschka died after a scalpel cut during an autopsy, Semmelweis made everyone wash in chlorinated lime, and deaths fell to about one percent. So why did the doctors refuse to believe him?

In this video:
- The two maternity clinics of Vienna and the deadly one
- The priest's bell and the other theories Semmelweis ruled out
- Kolletschka's scalpel and the cadaverous particles idea
- The chlorine bowl and the drop in childbed fever deaths
- Why doctors rejected handwashing, and the Semmelweis reflex

Subscribe to Stickstory for more true stories that changed the world. Would you have believed Semmelweis in 1847? Tell me in the comments!

#semmelweis #handwashing #medicalhistory #humanbody #stickstory

scenes.text: Vienna, 1846. A young woman in labor stands at the gate of the biggest hospital in the city, and she is begging.
scenes.visual: Snowy night street in front of the long two-storey Vienna General Hospital with rows of windows and a big arched iron gate; a gas lamp glows on the left; a pregnant young woman in a blue shawl walks up to the gate, and on 'begging' she reaches out with both hands; a doctor in a dark coat stands in the gate; note 'Vienna, 1846'.

scenes.text: Not for a doctor. She is begging, on her knees, not to be taken to the ward with the doctors.
scenes.visual: Closer at the gate: the woman in the blue shawl kneels in the snow, hands raised, face worried; the doctor beside the gate points inside.

scenes.text: Because everyone in Vienna knew something the doctors didn't. In that ward, mothers died.
scenes.visual: Inside a long ward: a row of five iron beds with mothers resting under blankets, curtains swaying; red placard 'FIRST CLINIC' high on the wall; on 'died' the middle bed slowly empties and a small candle is lit beside it.

scenes.text: So why was the clinic with the best-trained doctors the deadliest place to give birth?
scenes.visual: The hospital at night, a few windows glowing gold; the fez narrator walks in from the right, stops in front of the gate and holds up a sign 'WHY?' on 'deadliest' with raised brows.

scenes.text: The answer was hiding in plain sight, but it would cost one man everything.
scenes.visual: Close-up: one doctor's hand in a black coat cuff hovers over a white basin; a few red-brown stains on the back of the hand; on 'sight' a hand-written note 'the answer?' with an arrow to the hands.

scenes.text: The hospital had two maternity clinics, side by side.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 1 / 6 card: blue disc with 1, title 'Two Clinics'.

scenes.text: The First Clinic trained medical students. The Second Clinic trained midwives.
scenes.visual: A ward split by a wall: left placard 'FIRST CLINIC' (red) with a doctor and a medical student between the beds; right placard 'SECOND CLINIC' (blue) with a midwife in a bonnet and apron; each placard drops in as it is named.

scenes.text: And yet, in 1846, about one mother in nine who gave birth in the First Clinic died. In the Second Clinic, fewer than three in a hundred.
scenes.visual: A big case-notes sheet pinned to the ward wall, a desk edge with a candle and inkwell in front: title 'Deaths in 1846'; column 'First Clinic' with a long red bar '11.4%', column 'Second Clinic' with a short blue bar '2.8%'; red pill 'about 1 in 9' on 'nine'.

scenes.text: The killer was childbed fever. It struck a few days after the birth, and then, very often, death.
scenes.visual: Close on one bed in the ward: a mother resting under a blanket; red note 'childbed fever' on 'fever'; on 'death' the bed empties softly and a candle is lit.

scenes.text: So women did the math. Some gave birth on the street on purpose, and arrived afterwards.
scenes.visual: A snowy street, the hospital far on the right: a pregnant woman in a blue shawl walks slowly from right to left in the falling snow, away from the gate; note 'born on the street' on 'street' and, on 'afterwards', blue note 'arrive later'.

scenes.text: And here's the strange part. Those street births almost never got the fever.
scenes.visual: Snowy street by a gas lamp: a mother in a blue shawl stands holding her bundled baby; the fez narrator beside her jumps back in shock, then holds up a sign 'NO FEVER?!' on 'fever'.

scenes.text: So what did the First Clinic have that a cold street didn't?
scenes.visual: Giant words 'What did' / 'the ward have?' word by word, 'ward' in a red box; small note 'First Clinic'.

note.text: First Clinic vs. a cold street

scenes.text: In July 1846, a young Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis became an assistant in the First Clinic.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 2 / 6 card: blue disc with 2, title 'The Hunt'.

scenes.text: And the deaths haunted him. He started treating the wards like a crime scene.
scenes.visual: The ward with five beds, two of them empty with candles; young Dr. Semmelweis (dark coat, short beard) walks in and stops, worried, then points at the beds; note 'Ignaz Semmelweis' and red 'crime scene'.

scenes.text: Was it crowding? No. The Second Clinic was even more crowded.
scenes.visual: The case-notes sheet on the wall, desk in front: title 'Suspects'; first line 'too crowded?' crossed out in red on 'No'; blue pill 'Second Clinic: busier'.

scenes.text: Then he noticed the priest. To reach the dying, the priest walked through the First Clinic ringing a little bell.
scenes.visual: The ward: a priest in a long black cassock with a white collar walks slowly between the beds from left to right, ringing a small gold bell that sways and rings; the mothers lie still; note 'the priest's bell'.

scenes.text: Maybe the women were frightened to death? So Semmelweis asked him to take another route, with no bell. Nothing changed.
scenes.visual: Close in the ward: the fez narrator stands by a bed, hand on chin thinking, then holds up a sign 'NO BELL' on 'route'; on 'Nothing' he shrugs while red stamp 'NO CHANGE' lands on the wall.

scenes.text: In the Second Clinic, women gave birth lying on their side. He tried that too. Nothing.
scenes.visual: The case-notes sheet: 'Ideas he tested' with three lines crossed out one after another: 'too crowded?', 'the priest's bell?', 'lying on the side?' (on 'Nothing'); red pill 'Still dying'.

scenes.text: And then, in March 1847, the answer came from a death nobody expected.
scenes.visual: Horizontal time line: 'July 1846: Semmelweis arrives', 'March 1847: a death' (red); the marker jumps to March 1847 on 'March'.

scenes.text: Jakob Kolletschka was a professor and a good friend of Semmelweis.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 3 / 6 card: blue disc with 3, title 'The Scalpel'.

scenes.text: During an autopsy, a student's scalpel slipped and nicked his finger. A tiny cut. Within days, Kolletschka was dead.
scenes.visual: Close-up: one hand in a black coat cuff; a scalpel slides in from the upper right and grazes the fingertip on 'nicked', leaving a tiny red mark and one red drop; note 'Jakob Kolletschka'; on 'dead' a dark note 'March 1847'.

scenes.text: Semmelweis read the autopsy report, and his blood ran cold.
scenes.visual: A desk at night with a candle, a thick red book 'REPORT' and a quill scratching; Semmelweis stands at the right of the desk, reading, then jumps back in shock on 'cold'.

scenes.text: Inside, his friend's body looked just like the mothers'.
scenes.visual: The case-notes sheet: two columns 'Kolletschka' and 'The mothers', each with 'fever' and 'inflammation' ticked; red pill 'The same killer'.

scenes.text: Something from a dead body got in through a cut.
scenes.visual: Giant words 'Through' / 'a cut' word by word, 'cut' in a red box; the fez narrator on the right, hand on chin, then points at the words on 'cut'.

scenes.text: And who touched dead bodies every morning? The doctors and students of the First Clinic.
scenes.visual: A long vaulted hospital corridor: a dark door on the left under red plate 'AUTOPSY', a pale door on the right under blue plate 'MOTHERS'; a doctor and two students step out of the autopsy door on 'doctors'.

scenes.text: They did autopsies, then walked down the corridor and examined women in labor.
scenes.visual: The same corridor: a doctor walks from the autopsy door to the mothers' door; dotted footprints follow him and faint red specks drift from his hands along the way; red note 'unwashed hands' on 'examined'.

scenes.text: The midwives never did autopsies. And the women on the street? Nobody examined them at all.
scenes.visual: The split ward again: the right side lights up as a midwife in a bonnet waves; note 'no autopsies' with an arrow to her; on 'Nobody' a blue note 'street: no exams'.

scenes.text: Semmelweis called it cadaverous particles. He couldn't see them. But maybe he could wash them away.
scenes.visual: A brass microscope on the left; a big round field of view opens on the right, empty except for drifting grey question marks; note 'cadaverous particles' on 'cadaverous', blue 'wash them away?' on 'wash'.

scenes.text: In May 1847, he put a bowl at the door of the ward.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 4 / 6 card: blue disc with 4, title 'The Chlorine Bowl'.

scenes.text: It held chlorinated lime, a kind of bleach. Every doctor and student had to scrub in it before touching a patient.
scenes.visual: The corridor by the mothers' door: a wash stand with a white bowl of pale green liquid pops up on 'held'; note 'chlorinated lime'; a doctor walks up to it and holds his hands over it on 'scrub'.

scenes.text: It stung. And it worked.
scenes.visual: Close-up: the two hands dip into the bowl and scrub; the pale green liquid ripples, bubbles rise, the red specks fade away; on 'worked' a green stamp 'IT WORKED' lands.

scenes.text: In April, almost one mother in five in the First Clinic had died. By June, about two in a hundred. In 1848, the whole year ended at just over one percent.
scenes.visual: A full-frame ledger page with a hand-drawn red line: 'Apr 1847' at 18.3%, dropping steeply after a red vertical line 'chlorine' to 'Jun 1847' 2.2%, 'Jul' 1.2%, and '1848' 1.3%.

scenes.text: You'd think Vienna would carry him through the streets. Instead, the doctors turned on him!
scenes.visual: The hospital front by day: the fez narrator waves happily with a sign 'HERO?'; on 'turned' three doctors in dark coats in front of the gate turn their backs, and the narrator jumps in shock.

scenes.text: In 1847, nobody knew germs existed.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 5 / 6 card: blue disc with 5, title 'Why They Said No'.

scenes.text: Semmelweis could show that washing worked, but he couldn't explain why.
scenes.visual: The microscope and its empty round field of view with drifting question marks; note 'it works' in green, then red 'but why?' on 'why'.

scenes.text: And his idea carried a terrible message: the doctors were bringing death on their own hands.
scenes.visual: Close-up: the doctor's hands over the basin, red specks on the fingers; on 'hands' a red note 'their own hands' with an arrow.

scenes.text: Many of them were offended. Doctors were gentlemen, and a gentleman's hands were not dirty.
scenes.visual: The hospital corridor by the wash stand: three doctors in dark coats, one grey-bearded, stand with angry brows; one points away from the bowl, another shrugs; blue stamp 'gentlemen' on 'gentlemen', red note 'not dirty!' on 'dirty'.

scenes.text: His boss, Professor Johann Klein, never accepted it. And for years, Semmelweis barely published a word.
scenes.visual: A desk at night with a candle and a thick red book with a blank cover; grey-bearded Professor Johann Klein stands at the right with angry brows, arms folded into a shrug; note 'Prof. Johann Klein'; on 'published' a red note 'almost nothing in print'.

scenes.text: In 1849, Klein refused to renew his post. Semmelweis went home to Pest, in Hungary, and at Saint Rochus Hospital he did it again.
scenes.visual: Horizontal time line: '1849: post not renewed' (red), '1850: home to Pest', '1851: St. Rochus Hospital' (marker jumps along as each is named).

scenes.text: And childbed fever almost vanished.
scenes.visual: A brighter ward in Pest: warm window light falls across the floor, a door with a wash stand and a green chlorine bowl beside it, placard 'ST. ROCHUS, PEST' (red), four beds with mothers resting, none empty; the fez narrator points at the bowl, then waves happily on 'vanished'.

scenes.text: In 1861 he finally wrote his book. Critics tore it apart, and he answered with furious open letters, calling them murderers.
scenes.visual: The desk: a thick red book '1861' with a quill scratching; Semmelweis at the right turns angry on 'furious'; two letters fly up from the desk, each stamped 'OPEN LETTER' in red.

scenes.text: By 1865, his mind was failing. He was taken to an asylum in Vienna, and two weeks later he was dead, at only 47.
scenes.visual: A quiet snowy night in Vienna: a low, dark asylum building behind iron railings with spear tips, a closed iron gate, only one window lit gold, a gas lamp; soft snow falls; note 'Vienna, 1865' and, on 'dead', 'age 47'.

scenes.text: The cause? An infected wound.
scenes.visual: Giant words 'An infected' / 'wound' word by word, 'infected' in a red box.

scenes.text: And here's the cruel part. Within twenty years, the world caught up.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 6 / 6 card: blue disc with 6, title 'Proven Right'.

scenes.text: Joseph Lister began cleaning wounds with antiseptic. Louis Pasteur showed that tiny living germs cause disease.
scenes.visual: The microscope; Louis Pasteur (dark coat, short beard) stands beside it pointing; first a note 'Joseph Lister: antiseptic' on 'Lister', then 'Louis Pasteur' on 'Pasteur', and the round field of view fills with wriggling red rod-shaped germs on 'germs'.

scenes.text: Germs explained everything Semmelweis had seen. Today he's called the savior of mothers.
scenes.visual: The corridor between 'AUTOPSY' and 'MOTHERS': red specks drift in the air along the footprints; the fez narrator points at them, then on 'savior' holds up a sign 'SAVIOR OF MOTHERS'.

scenes.text: There's even a name for what happened to him: the Semmelweis reflex, rejecting new evidence because it clashes with old beliefs.
scenes.visual: The case-notes sheet titled 'The Semmelweis reflex': 'new evidence arrives' (tick), 'it clashes with old beliefs' (cross), 'rejected anyway' (cross); blue pill 'Still happens today'.

scenes.text: So why was the best ward in Vienna the deadliest? Because of the doctors' own hands.
scenes.visual: The First Clinic ward once more: a doctor with red specks on his hands walks between the beds towards a mother; on 'hands' a red note 'their own hands' with an arrow to his hands.

scenes.text: And the cure was a bowl of bleach, plus the courage to admit you might be the problem.
scenes.visual: The corridor: the fez narrator walks to the wash stand with the bowl, washes, then points at himself; note 'a bowl of bleach' and, on 'courage', blue 'and courage'.

scenes.text: Would you have believed him in 1847? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe to Stickstory for more true stories that changed the world.
scenes.visual: The hospital gate on a snowy evening, windows glowing gold: the fez narrator holds up a sign 'WOULD YOU?', then waves goodbye on 'subscribe'.
